lesson.title: Reading the Integral Sign
lesson.summary: The symbol ∫f(x)dx is the standard shorthand for an indefinite integral, and each piece of it carries specific meaning worth learning to read fluently.
lesson.body:
You have already been using the notation ∫f(x)dx in the previous chapter to represent an indefinite integral, but it is worth slowing down and learning to read every piece of it, the same way you once learned to read f'(x) or dy/dx for derivatives.

The elongated S shape, ∫, is called the integral sign. It was introduced by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in the late seventeenth century as a stretched-out letter S, standing for the Latin word 'summa,' meaning sum. Integration and summation are historically and conceptually linked, since accumulating a quantity through integration behaves like adding up infinitely many small pieces. For the indefinite integral, you can think of the integral sign as an instruction: 'find the family of antiderivatives of what follows.'

Immediately after the integral sign comes a function, and at the end comes an expression like dx. Both of these pieces have their own names and their own chapters coming up, so for now just notice their positions: the function right after ∫ is the thing being integrated, and the dx at the end tells you which variable the process is being performed with respect to. Together, ∫, the function, and the dx form one complete instruction that cannot be split apart and still mean the same thing.

Let's read a full example piece by piece using the family you already verified: ∫3x^2 dx = x^3 + C. The ∫ says 'find the indefinite integral.' The 3x^2 is the function being integrated. The dx says the integration is being performed with respect to x. And the right-hand side, x^3 + C, is the answer: the general antiderivative. If you differentiate x^3 + C, you land back on 3x^2, which is the check that confirms the notation was used correctly.

Learning to read this notation fluently matters because every rule you learn from here forward, the power rule, the sum rule, the difference rule, and beyond, will be stated using this exact symbolic language. Being comfortable identifying the integral sign, the function being integrated, and the variable of integration on sight will make each new rule far easier to absorb.
